clinicalPearls: The U.S. ATSDR ranks arsenic, lead, mercury, and cadmium as the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 7th most hazardous substances at toxic waste sites; the WHO lists all four among the 10 chemicals of greatest public-health concern globally (Harrison 22e p.3699).
Lead and mercury are xenobiotic metals with no clear safe threshold, whereas copper and selenium are essential trace elements that become toxic only at high exposure (Harrison 22e p.3699).

Acute arsenic poisoning produces hemorrhagic gastroenteritis with intestinal mucosal necrosis, fluid loss and hypotension, plus delayed cardiomyopathy, acute tubular necrosis, and hemolysis; chronic exposure causes peripheral neuropathy, hyperkeratosis/hyperpigmentation, and cancers of skin, lung, liver (angiosarcoma), bladder, and kidney (Harrison 22e p.3700).
Classic arsenic signs include a garlicky breath odor and Mees' lines (transverse white striae on the fingernails); arsenic is radiopaque and may be visible on abdominal x-ray (Harrison 22e p.3700).

Cadmium has a biologic half-life of 10-30 years; severe food/water contamination in Japan caused itai-itai (ouch-ouch) disease with painful bone fractures from cadmium-induced bone toxicity (Harrison 22e p.3699-3700).

Lead in blood is 95-99% sequestered in red cells, so lead must be measured in whole blood rather than serum; about 15% of an absorbed dose is stored in bone with a half-life >20 years, making bone (KXRF) levels a marker of cumulative exposure (Harrison 22e p.3700).

Impairment of childhood IQ from lead occurs with no measurable threshold down to the assay limit of detection (~1 ug/dL); the CDC recommends screening children at about 6 months and intervening if blood lead exceeds 3.5 ug/dL (Harrison 22e p.3700).

Chronic metallic mercury vapor exposure produces an intention tremor and mercurial erethism (excitability, memory loss, insomnia, timidity, delirium) -- the historical 'mad as a hatter' picture (Harrison 22e p.3701).

Children exposed to mercury in any form may develop acrodynia ('pink disease'): flushing, itching, swelling, tachycardia, hypertension, excessive salivation/perspiration, irritability, weakness, and desquamation of palms and soles (Harrison 22e p.3701).
Dimethylmercury is 'supertoxic' -- a few drops absorbed through skin or inhaled can cause fatal cerebellar degeneration (Harrison 22e p.3701).

Manganese overexposure (miners, welders, dry-battery workers) causes a parkinsonian syndrome within 1-2 years that, unlike idiopathic Parkinson disease, is nonresponsive to L-dopa (Harrison 22e p.3702).
The single most important treatment is recognizing and stopping the exposure; activated charcoal does not bind metals and is of limited value in acute metal ingestion (Harrison 22e p.3699).
harrison.pathophysiology: Metals enter the body chiefly by inhalation of dusts/fumes, ingestion of contaminated food or water (especially via hand-to-mouth activity in children), and sometimes vapor (e.g., mercury) or dermal absorption (organic lead, thallium). Gastrointestinal absorption varies markedly with the chemical form of the metal and host nutritional status. Once absorbed, metals are transported in blood and sequestered in organs such as bone, liver, and kidney, sometimes for years, then excreted mainly by renal and gastrointestinal routes (with minor losses via sweat, saliva, breath, milk, skin, hair, and nails). Toxicity arises from enzyme inhibition, damage to subcellular organelles and DNA, covalent protein modification, generation of reactive oxygen species, and displacement of essential metals from metal-dependent proteins; metals also alter DNA methylation and other epigenetic marks, dysregulating gene and microRNA expression. Many metals bind sulfhydryl (thiol) groups; cadmium and mercury both bind cellular sulfhydryls, cadmium competing with zinc and calcium, and lead interferes with mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, ATPases, and calcium-dependent messengers while enhancing oxidation and apoptosis. Genetic polymorphisms affecting metal binding/transport and nutritional/comorbid factors modify individual susceptibility (Harrison 22e p.3699-3700).
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of acute gastroenteritis with hemodynamic collapse (arsenic, mercuric salt, or cadmium ingestion)
Acquired peripheral polyneuropathy from other toxic/metabolic causes (arsenic, thallium, lead)
Parkinsonism from other causes (manganese-induced parkinsonism vs idiopathic Parkinson disease)
Microcytic/normocytic anemia from other causes (lead-related anemia with basophilic stippling; cadmium-related microcytic hypochromic anemia unresponsive to iron)
Encephalopathy of other etiology (lead encephalopathy; aluminum-related dialysis encephalopathy)
Fanconi syndrome / proximal tubulopathy from other nephrotoxins
infectionMimics: Bacterial or viral gastroenteritis (mimicked by acute arsenic, mercuric salt, or cadmium ingestion)
Pneumonia (mimicked by acute cadmium or mercury vapor inhalation causing pneumonitis/noncardiogenic pulmonary edema)
nonInfectiousMimics: Iron-deficiency anemia (cadmium-induced anemia unresponsive to iron)
Pyelonephritis and other renal disease causing elevated urinary beta-2-microglobulin (overlaps with cadmium nephropathy marker)
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and hearing loss (associations described with lead)
additionalInvestigations: 24-h urinary arsenic (toxic >67 umol/d or 50 ug/d, after 24 h without seafood); serum arsenic >0.9 umol/L (7 ug/dL) if recent; arsenic in hair/nails
Whole-blood lead level (not serum); blood protoporphyrin (free erythrocyte or zinc); peripheral smear for basophilic stippling; nerve conduction studies; long-bone x-ray for epiphyseal 'lead lines'
KXRF (in vivo x-ray fluorescence) bone lead measurement to assess cumulative lead exposure
Serum cadmium >500 nmol/L (5 ug/dL) if recent; urinary cadmium >100 nmol/L (10 ug/g creatinine); urinary beta-2-microglobulin >750 ug/g creatinine
Blood mercury (recent) or hair mercury (chronic organic exposure); urine mercury; provocation: >20-ug rise in 24-h urine mercury after a 2-g succimer dose for remote exposure
ECG (arsenic: QRS broadening, QT prolongation, ST depression, T-wave flattening); abdominal x-ray for radiopaque arsenic or thallium
redFlags: Acute encephalopathy with convulsions and coma at very high blood lead (>80-120 ug/dL) -- risk of death
Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema after acute cadmium or mercury-vapor inhalation
Hemorrhagic gastroenteritis with hypotension and delayed cardiomyopathy in acute arsenic poisoning
Cardiovascular collapse after acute ingestion of inorganic mercury (lethal dose 10-42 mg/kg)
Garlicky breath, Mees' lines, or a gingival 'lead line' indicating significant metal exposure
Skin or inhalational exposure to dimethylmercury (supertoxic; minute amounts fatal)
Pregnancy exposure to mercury or high maternal bone lead -- risk of severe fetal neurodevelopmental injury
harrison.prognosis: Outcome depends on the metal, dose, acuity, and promptness of exposure termination. Acute high-dose poisoning can be fatal (e.g., lead encephalopathy at BPb >120 ug/dL; inorganic mercury ingestion at 10-42 mg/kg; cadmium or mercury-vapor pulmonary edema; dimethylmercury exposure). Many effects of chronic exposure are irreversible or only partly reversible, including peripheral neuropathy, cognitive decline, manganese parkinsonism (L-dopa nonresponsive), itai-itai bone disease, and cadmium-related chronic renal failure for which no effective chelation exists. Cumulative lead burden is an established risk factor for chronic disease, including hypertension, cardiovascular morbidity/mortality, and chronic kidney disease, and prenatal exposure carries lasting offspring neurodevelopmental risk (Harrison 22e p.3699-3702).
pitfalls: Measuring lead in serum instead of whole blood (95-99% of lead is in red cells) (Harrison 22e p.3700).

Relying on activated charcoal for metal ingestion -- charcoal does not bind metals (Harrison 22e p.3699); however thallium is an exception, where charcoal interrupts enterohepatic circulation (Harrison 22e p.3702).
Attributing high urinary beta-2-microglobulin solely to cadmium -- it also rises in other renal diseases such as pyelonephritis (Harrison 22e p.3700).
Misreading elevated total arsenic from recent seafood (nontoxic organic arsenobetaine/arsenocholine) as toxic inorganic arsenic -- test after 24 h without seafood (Harrison 22e p.3700).
Attempting chelation for cadmium poisoning -- chelation is not useful and dimercaprol can worsen cadmium nephrotoxicity (Harrison 22e p.3700).
Expecting chelation to improve outcomes in asymptomatic childhood lead exposure -- a large randomized trial showed no benefit on intelligence at BPb 20-40 ug/dL (Harrison 22e p.3700).
Mistaking manganese parkinsonism for idiopathic Parkinson disease and expecting an L-dopa response (Harrison 22e p.3702).
harrison.severityClassification: No single unified grading; severity is metal- and level-specific. Lead: subclinical childhood effects at BPb ~25-60 ug/dL, with IQ impairment down to ~1 ug/dL; clinically apparent neurodevelopmental delay at BPb 40-80 ug/dL; acute impaired neurotransmission/neuronal death at BPb >60-80 ug/dL; acute encephalopathy with convulsions/coma at BPb >80-120 ug/dL. Adult occupational removal at BPb >40 ug/dL (proposed newer target <10 ug/dL, removal if >20 ug/dL). Arsenic lethal dose 120-200 mg in adults, 2 mg/kg in children. Inorganic mercury ingestion lethal at 10-42 mg/kg; organic mercury CNS lesions at >1.7 mg/kg. Thallium severe poisoning after single dose >1 g or >8 mg/kg (Harrison 22e p.3700-3702).
management: Immediately identify and terminate the source of exposure, whether occupational, environmental or dietary, as the essential first step
Chelate significant arsenic or inorganic lead poisoning with agents such as succimer (DMSA), dimercaprol (BAL) or DMPS, guided by the metal involved and clinical severity
Treat lead encephalopathy with parenteral dimercaprol combined with calcium disodium edetate and manage cerebral oedema
Chelate mercury burden with succimer or DMPS, avoiding dimercaprol in organic (methyl) mercury exposure, and consider Prussian blue for thallium
Provide aggressive supportive care with fluid resuscitation and electrolyte correction for arsenical haemorrhagic gastroenteritis, plus cardiac monitoring for arsenic-induced arrhythmia
Monitor and support renal function given the risk of acute tubular necrosis, and follow serial blood and urinary metal concentrations to gauge chelation
Involve a clinical toxicologist or poisons service and, for childhood lead exposure, arrange environmental abatement and public-health notification
